# Automatic and Data-Driven Generation
## Overview
This family encompasses methods that generate or assign transfer functions (TFs) algorithmically, removing or reducing the need for manual user interaction [G]. Unlike [Classification and transfer functions](38-classification-and-transfer-functions.md) which provides the general framework for mapping data to optical properties, these methods automate the selection of mapping parameters [G]. They differ from [Transfer Function Optimization and Learning](5933-transfer-function-optimization-and-learning.md) by often focusing on initial generation or retrieval rather than iterative feedback loops, and from [Default 3D Transfer Function](5647-default-3d-transfer-function.md) by employing diverse strategies such as statistical modeling, generative adversarial networks, or knowledge-base retrieval [G].
## Shared principles
Builds on the classification mechanism of [Classification and transfer functions](38-classification-and-transfer-functions.md), which evaluates a classification function $C(\mathbf{x})$ for each sample point to produce optical properties [G].
## Subtopics

### [Default 3D Transfer Function](5647-default-3d-transfer-function.md)
Generates a starting-point visualization without user interaction by prioritizing edge detection over statistical clustering. It is chosen when a geometrically grounded baseline for manual refinement is needed, distinguishing materials with overlapping intensity ranges via gradient and curvature. [G]

### [Histogram-Based Transfer Function Generation](6182-histogram-based-transfer-function-generation.md)
Automatically derives opacity and color mappings by analyzing statistical distributions of volumetric data values and derivatives. It is chosen to identify critical intensity thresholds directly from histogram peaks, reducing user interaction compared to manual design. [G]

### [Valley Cell-Based Clustering Transfer Function Design](7418-valley-cell-based-clustering-transfer-function-design.md)
Automatically generates 2D opacity transfer functions by decomposing feature density plots into topological "valley cells" and mapping them to Gaussian functions. It is chosen to automatically determine feature counts and hierarchically simplify classification, removing noise while preserving significant structures. [G]

### [Opacity GAN](7664-opacity-gan.md)
A generative model that synthesizes a 64×64 opacity image from viewpoint and opacity transfer function inputs. It is chosen to capture general shape and silhouette, enabling introspection on inputs for analysis of the latent space. [G]

### [Opacity-to-Color Translation GAN](7665-opacity-to-color-translation-gan.md)
A conditional generative adversarial network that synthesizes a high-resolution color image conditioned on viewpoint, color TF, opacity TF, and an opacity image. It is chosen to solve automatic color mapping by treating the task as an image-to-image translation problem. [G]

### [Gaussian Mixture Model Transfer Function Generation](7676-gaussian-mixture-model-transfer-function-generation.md)
Generates diverse training data or initial TFs by sampling parameters from a prior distribution using a Gaussian Mixture Model. It is chosen to provide a broad initial exploration of the rendering space without user interaction, differing from histogram-based methods by being data-independent. [G]

### SOI Label-Based Knowledge Database Construction
Builds a retrieval database using raw image volumes and SOI labels instead of expert-designed TFs [S2, unofficial]. It automatically extracts rays from raw volumes, generates TIQ (Two-Image Query) representations from the rays, and stores TIQs and associated SOI labels in the knowledge database [S2, unofficial]. It differs from expert TF collection by relying on SOI labels, which requires less effort and time to generate [S2, unofficial]. It is chosen to rapidly retrieve and adapt existing visualizations based on structural similarity, requiring less effort than manual TF collection [S2, unofficial].

### Probability-Intensity Renderer
Assigns optical properties based on predicted ROI-wise class probabilities via a weighted sum of all $N$ ROI classes [S3, unofficial]. It incorporates voxel intensity $I(v)$ into TF design, using predicted probabilities as visibility weights and applying a threshold $\tau_n$ to suppress low-confidence contributions [S3, unofficial]. It calculates the total weight $W(v) = \sum_{n: p_n(v) \ge \tau_n} p_n(v)$, summing probabilities of classes above the threshold [S3, unofficial]. The final color and opacity are computed as $C(v) = \frac{1}{W(v)} \sum_{n: p_n(v) \ge \tau_n} \text{TF}_{c,n}(I(v)) \cdot p_n(v)$ and $\alpha(v) = \frac{1}{W(v)} \sum_{n: p_n(v) \ge \tau_n} \text{TF}_{\alpha,n}(I(v)) \cdot p_n(v)$, where $\text{TF}_{c,n}$ and $\text{TF}_{\alpha,n}$ are functions of intensity $I(v)$ [S3, unofficial]. The threshold $\tau_n$ is a predefined value to suppress low-confidence contributions, though its exact numerical value is not specified [S3, unofficial]. It is chosen to allow intuitive assignment of optical properties based on confidence levels, though it may suppress fine details (e.g., small vessels, lung bronchus) because intensity variation within the same ROI is not considered [S3, unofficial].

### Diffusion Models (DDPMs)
DDPMs generate data by learning to reverse a gradual noising process, iteratively denoising from pure noise to a data distribution sample [S4, unofficial]. Diffusion models have applications spanning volume generation, Transfer Function (TF) design, and visualization synthesis [S4, unofficial].

## Background
Automatic and data-driven generation methods emerged to address the labor-intensive nature of manual transfer function design [G]. Early approaches focused on histogram-based analysis to identify material boundaries [6182-histogram-based-transfer-function-generation.md]. More recent developments leverage machine learning, including generative models like GANs for synthesizing plausible visualizations [7664-opacity-gan.md], [7665-opacity-to-color-translation-gan.md] and probabilistic models for integrating semantic information [S3, unofficial]. Knowledge-base retrieval approaches have also been developed to reuse existing visualizations based on structural similarity [S2, unofficial]. Diffusion models have also been applied to TF design and visualization synthesis [S4, unofficial].
